full_title: PEOPLE OF THE PHILIPPINES, PLAINTIFF-APPELLEE, VS. JEORGE EJERCITO ESTREGAN, ARLYN LAZARO-TORRES, TERRYL GAMIT-TALABONG, KALAHI U. RABAGO, ERWIN P. SACLUTI, GENER C. DIMARANAN, AND MARILYN M. BRUEL, ACCUSED-APPELLANTS.
subject: Criminal Law
syllabus_topic: IV. Special Penal Laws > E. Anti-Graft and Corrupt Practices Act (RA 3019, as amended by BP 195 and RA 10910)
topics: Elements of Section 3(e), RA 3019: manifest partiality, evident bad faith, unwarranted benefits
Procurement violations do not per se establish Section 3(e)
Sanggunian members who authorize and ratify a contract are not automatically liable
Accident protection agreement as a contract of insurance (PD 612, Sec. 2)
Mode of appeal from Sandiganbayan judgments in original-jurisdiction criminal cases

other_subjects.subject: Commercial and Taxation Laws
other_subjects.syllabus_topic: II. Insurance Law > A. General Principles

other_subjects.subject: Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics

doctrine:
A violation of procurement laws, rules and regulations does **not per se** result in conviction under **Section 3(e) of RA 3019** (reiterated). The prosecution must still prove beyond reasonable doubt that:

- the accused is a public officer discharging administrative, judicial or official functions;
- the accused acted with manifest partiality, evident bad faith or gross inexcusable negligence; and
- the accused caused undue injury to any party, including the Government, or gave a private party unwarranted benefits, advantage or preference.

Under the second mode, the third element is met even without proof of damage. **A mayor who bypasses public bidding and contracts with an entity he knows lacks legal authority and any track record gives it unwarranted benefit with manifest partiality and evident bad faith.** The private party who conspires with him is equally liable. By contrast, **sanggunian members who merely pass an ordinance authorizing the mayor to contract with "any competent and qualified entity"** (even if it wrongly authorizes negotiated procurement) and later ratify the contract show no partiality toward a particular entity. This is especially so where the contract's validity did not depend on their resolution, which confers no rights.

An agreement by which one undertakes, for a consideration, to indemnify another against loss, damage or liability from an unknown or contingent event is a **contract of insurance** (PD 612, Sec. 2(1)). A memorandum of agreement under which a firm indemnifies tourists and boatmen for accidental death or dismemberment, and reimburses the municipality's medical expenses up to scheduled amounts, is accident insurance, because indemnity is its principal object. The absence of a separately labeled premium is not conclusive. As "goods" under RA 9184, such a contract must be procured by competitive bidding unless a ground for an alternative method exists. Procedurally, a Sandiganbayan judgment in a criminal case within its original jurisdiction is appealed to the Supreme Court by **notice of appeal** (2018 Revised Internal Rules of the Sandiganbayan, Rule IX, Sec. 1(a)).
facts:
The Sangguniang Bayan (SB) of Pagsanjan, Laguna passed Municipal Ordinance No. 15-2008. It authorized Mayor Jeorge Ejercito Estregan to negotiate and contract with "any competent and qualified entity" for accident protection and assistance (APA) to tourists and boatmen on boat rides in the Pagsanjan Gorge Tourist Zone. On September 22, 2008, First Rapids Care Ventures (FRCV), owned by Marilyn Bruel, submitted a written proposal. Without public bidding, Estregan signed a memorandum of agreement (MOA) with FRCV on October 23, 2008. The SB ratified it the same day through Municipal Resolution No. 056-2008. Under the MOA, FRCV would indemnify tourists and boatmen for accidental death or dismemberment, and reimburse the municipality for actual treatment or confinement expenses up to the amounts in its tables of coverage. The APA fee of PHP 48.00 per tourist was part of a PHP 160.00 boat-ride ticket. The municipal treasurer collected the fee, and FRCV's share was remitted to it by check.

FRCV had no Certificate of Authority from the Insurance Commission. It was registered with the DTI only on March 19, 2008 and with the BIR only on September 17, 2008, five days before its offer, and its BIR-registered line of business was "Other Computer Related Activities." Bruel had been an insurance agent of Malayan Insurance before forming FRCV. Estregan said Philamlife and Oriental Insurance had made inquiries but could not meet all the program's requirements.

On a 2009 complaint by the United Boatmen Association of Pagsanjan, the Ombudsman found probable cause. On March 16, 2016, an Information for violation of Section 3(e) of RA 3019 was filed with the Sandiganbayan against the mayor, the vice mayor, six councilors and Bruel; the complaint against one councilor had been dismissed by reason of his death. The prosecution's sole witness identified the Insurance Commissioner's letter-opinion that the MOA is a contract of insurance. The councilors testified that the Bids and Awards Committee (BAC) refused to act because there was no approved budget for the contract. The Sandiganbayan found that the legal opinions they relied on were sought only after the MOA had been signed and ratified.

In its April 5, 2019 Decision in SB-16-CRM-0124, the Sandiganbayan acquitted Vice Mayor Vilar. It convicted Estregan, Councilors Torres, Talabong, Rabago, Sacluti and Dimaranan, and Bruel, and sentenced each to an indeterminate prison term with perpetual disqualification from public office. It denied reconsideration on July 5, 2019, and the convicted accused appealed. The OSP argued that they had used the wrong mode of appeal. Estregan's new counsel filed his brief more than three years after the Court granted him additional time.
issues: Whether accused-appellants used the correct mode of appeal from the Sandiganbayan.
Whether the MOA is a contract of insurance whose procurement required public bidding under RA 9184.
Whether Estregan and Bruel are guilty beyond reasonable doubt of violating Section 3(e) of RA 3019.
Whether SB members Torres, Talabong, Rabago, Sacluti and Dimaranan are guilty beyond reasonable doubt of violating Section 3(e) of RA 3019.
ruling:
**1. Yes, a notice of appeal was the correct mode.** The case was decided by the Sandiganbayan in its original jurisdiction. Under Rule IX, Sec. 1(a) of the 2018 Revised Internal Rules of the Sandiganbayan, which prevail over the procedure in PD 1606 (*People v. Talaue*), the appeal is by notice of appeal. The Court rejected the excuses of Estregan's counsel. Rule 7, Sec. 3 of the 2019 Amended Rules requires written submissions to be signed, and counsel's earlier motion was unsigned. Filing the brief more than three years after the extension "betrays his negligence, if not abandonment, of the appeal." In any case, the appeal failed on the merits.

**2. Yes, the MOA is an insurance contract that had to be bid out.** The MOA "unmistakably" shows that FRCV undertook to indemnify tourists and boatmen for accidental death or dismemberment, and the municipality for medical expenses up to stated limits. Bruel cited *Philippine Health Care Providers, Inc. v. CIR* (no insurance business where indemnity is merely incidental to service). That ruling does not apply, because indemnification was the MOA's principal object; training and assistance were incidental. Estregan's own testimony supported this: he had personally shouldered funeral and repatriation costs, and he first sought offers from insurance companies. An accident insurer, unlike a medical service provider, indemnifies only up to the scheduled rates, which is what FRCV did. As to the absence of a premium, PD 612, Sec. 2(2) states that the lack of profit or of a separate consideration is not conclusive. In any event, the "coverage outlay" of PHP 48.00 per tourist was the premium. Doing business "in substance equivalent" to insurance in a manner designed to evade the Code is still doing an insurance business.

An insurance contract is "goods" under Sec. 5(h) of RA 9184. Even if FRCV mainly trained boatmen, that would be consulting services, still within RA 9184. Competitive bidding is the default mode (Revised IRR, Rule IV, Sec. 10). Ordinance No. 15-2008 instead authorized negotiated procurement at once, although that method is allowed only in particular cases such as two failed biddings or emergencies (IRR, Sec. 53). None of those cases existed. Estregan claimed that the BAC and GPPB had said no bidding was needed, but that was a bare allegation. **The procurement law was violated.**

**3. Yes, Estregan and Bruel are guilty.** A procurement violation is not enough by itself, so the Court examined the elements. The first element (public officer) was undisputed. Section 3(e) may be committed by *dolo* (manifest partiality or evident bad faith) or *culpa* (gross inexcusable negligence). **Estregan acted with manifest partiality and evident bad faith.** He contracted with FRCV despite "glaringly questionable circumstances": its very recent DTI and BIR registrations and its lack of a Certificate of Authority. His claim that FRCV was the only qualified provider deserved scant consideration. The public consultations dealt only with increasing the boat-ride fee, not with FRCV's qualifications, which were the BAC's job "which Estregan arrogated upon himself." On the third element, "there is indeed no estimable proof of damage to any party." The element was nonetheless met under the second mode. **By sparing FRCV the procurement process and ignoring its irregularities, Estregan gave it unwarranted benefit, advantage or preference**, since FRCV had no legal authority to engage in insurance at all. **Bruel** fraudulently represented that FRCV was fully capable. It made no difference that she never called FRCV an insurer, because the MOA itself shows insurance business. FRCV's registrations showed it was created just for this contract. Even if FRCV performed under the MOA, that would not negate her fraud. She conspired with Estregan.

**4. No, the SB members are acquitted.** Ordinance No. 15-2008 referred to "any competent and qualified entity," which was yet to be determined. Even if the ordinance wrongly authorized negotiated procurement, it showed no partiality to any particular entity and did not prevent Estregan from holding a public bidding. Their ratification through Resolution No. 056-2008 did not make them liable either, because the MOA's validity did not depend on it. "No rights can be conferred by and be inferred from a resolution, which is but an embodiment of what the lawmaking body has to say in light of attendant circumstances."
disposition: The appeal was PARTLY GRANTED. The Sandiganbayan's April 5, 2019 Decision and July 5, 2019 Resolution in SB-16-CRM-0124 were AFFIRMED as to Jeorge Ejercito Estregan and Marilyn M. Bruel. Both were found GUILTY beyond reasonable doubt of violating Section 3(e) of RA 3019 and sentenced to an indeterminate penalty of six years and one month, as minimum, to eight years, as maximum, with perpetual disqualification from holding public office. The Decision and Resolution were MODIFIED as to Arlyn Lazaro-Torres, Terryl Gamit-Talabong, Kalahi U. Rabago, Erwin P. Sacluti and Gener C. Dimaranan, who were ACQUITTED on reasonable doubt. Entry of judgment was ordered as to the acquitted accused-appellants.

bar_questions.q: A municipal ordinance authorized Mayor Dante to contract with "any competent and qualified entity" for accident protection of tourists. Without public bidding, Dante signed an agreement with XYZ Ventures, a sole proprietorship that had registered with the BIR only five days before submitting its offer and held no certificate of authority from the Insurance Commission. Under the agreement, XYZ would indemnify tourists for accidental death and reimburse the town's medical expenses up to fixed amounts, in exchange for a fixed share of every boat-ride ticket. Charged with violating Section 3(e) of RA 3019, Dante argues that he cannot be convicted because the town suffered no actual damage: XYZ paid every claim during the life of the contract. Is Dante's defense tenable?

alac.answer: No. Dante may be convicted even without proof of actual damage, because he gave XYZ unwarranted benefits, advantage or preference through manifest partiality and evident bad faith.
alac.legal_basis: Section 3(e) of RA 3019 punishes a public officer who, in the discharge of official functions and through manifest partiality, evident bad faith or gross inexcusable negligence, causes undue injury to any party or gives any private party unwarranted benefits, advantage or preference. The two modes are distinct; under the second, proof of damage is unnecessary. A procurement violation is not per se a Section 3(e) violation, but all the elements are present when a mayor bypasses the bidding process and contracts with an entity he knows lacks legal authority and a track record. (People v. Estregan, G.R. No. 248699, February 5, 2025)
alac.application: Dante is a public officer who acted in the discharge of his functions. The agreement is a contract of insurance, which is "goods" requiring competitive bidding under RA 9184, yet he dispensed with bidding. He chose an entity registered only days before its offer and without a certificate of authority from the Insurance Commission. Those glaring circumstances show a clear inclination to favor XYZ and a conscious wrongdoing, which are manifest partiality and evident bad faith. By sparing XYZ the rigors of procurement and letting it do an insurance business it had no authority to do, Dante gave it unwarranted benefit. XYZ's payment of claims does not erase that benefit, since the second mode does not require damage.
alac.conclusion: Dante's defense is untenable, and he may be convicted under the second mode of Section 3(e).

bar_questions.q: In the same case, Councilors Ella and Fe are also charged. Their only participation was (1) voting for the ordinance that authorized the mayor to negotiate and contract with "any competent and qualified entity" for accident protection, and (2) on the same day the mayor signed the agreement with XYZ, voting for a resolution ratifying it. The prosecution argues that the ordinance itself violated the procurement law by authorizing negotiated procurement when none of its grounds, such as two failed biddings or an emergency, existed. Are Ella and Fe liable under Section 3(e)?

alac.answer: No. Ella and Fe should be acquitted.
alac.legal_basis: A violation of procurement laws does not per se result in conviction under Section 3(e) of RA 3019; manifest partiality, evident bad faith or gross inexcusable negligence and the resulting injury or unwarranted benefit must be proved beyond reasonable doubt. SB members who pass an ordinance authorizing the mayor to contract with "any competent and qualified entity" do not show partiality toward any particular entity, even if the ordinance wrongly authorizes negotiated procurement. A ratifying resolution does not make them liable where the contract's validity does not depend on it, because a resolution confers no rights. (People v. Estregan, G.R. No. 248699, February 5, 2025)
alac.application: The ordinance did not name XYZ or any other entity, and it did not stop the mayor from holding a public bidding. Even assuming it erroneously authorized negotiated procurement, it shows no clear inclination to favor anyone. The choice of XYZ was the mayor's. The ratifying resolution was not needed for the agreement to be valid, so voting for it did not give XYZ the benefit. The prosecution has shown, at most, a procurement irregularity, not the elements of Section 3(e).
alac.conclusion: Ella and Fe are not liable under Section 3(e) and must be acquitted on reasonable doubt.

bar_questions.q: Bea's firm is not licensed by the Insurance Commission. Under its agreement with a municipality, it indemnifies tourists and boatmen for accidental death or dismemberment and reimburses the municipality's medical expenses up to scheduled amounts. The firm also trains boatmen and deploys first-aid and rescue teams. Bea contends that the agreement is a "special services" contract, not insurance, because (i) her firm renders services, and (ii) the agreement does not require the municipality to pay any "premium," only a "coverage outlay" of PHP 48.00 per tourist taken from each ticket. (a) Is the agreement a contract of insurance? (b) Was public bidding required to award it?

alac.answer: (a) Yes, it is a contract of insurance. (b) Yes, public bidding was required.
alac.legal_basis: A contract of insurance is an agreement whereby one undertakes for a consideration to indemnify another against loss, damage or liability arising from an unknown or contingent event (PD 612, Sec. 2(1)). The absence of profit or of a separate consideration is not conclusive. Doing business in substance equivalent to insurance in a manner designed to evade the Code is doing an insurance business (Sec. 2(2)). Where indemnification is the principal object and services are incidental, the contract is insurance. An insurance contract is "goods" under Sec. 5(h) of RA 9184, and procurement must be by competitive bidding unless an alternative method is justified by grounds such as two failed biddings or an emergency. Even training services would be consulting services covered by RA 9184. (People v. Estregan, G.R. No. 248699, February 5, 2025)
alac.application: (a) The firm's core undertaking is to pay for accidental death, dismemberment and medical expenses, all contingent events, up to scheduled limits. That is what an accident insurer does. The training and rescue teams are incidental to that indemnity. The "coverage outlay" of PHP 48.00 per tourist is the consideration for assuming the risk, so it is a premium in all but name. Calling the contract "special services" cannot avoid the Insurance Code. (b) As insurance, the contract is "goods" under RA 9184. If the services were the main object, they would be consulting services, also covered by RA 9184. Either way, competitive bidding was the required mode, and no ground for an alternative method appears.
alac.conclusion: The agreement is an insurance contract, and it could be awarded only through public bidding.

notes: The Sandiganbayan's summary of defense evidence refers to Ordinance No. 14-2008 (as amended by Ordinance No. 18-2008) for the fee schedule and also as the mayor's authority to contract. The stipulations and the Court's own discussion treat Ordinance No. 15-2008 as the authorizing ordinance, and this digest follows the Court. The Court criticized the late brief of Estregan's counsel but resolved Estregan's appeal on the merits; it did not expressly expunge the brief or dismiss his appeal for abandonment.
